Disturbing is the most commonly used word, barely edging out troubling. Mitt Romney was disturbed. Ben Sasse found the news troubling. Lindsey Graham was his sassy little southern self, claiming none of it was a problem. It makes you wonder what these guys would find distressing or even worrisome not to speak of appalling. They're not normally so understated. For example, remember them claiming against the toddler hordes of gang members, pouring across our borders, pronouncing it was a war, an invasion, and a disgusting threat to our way of life? For once, the Democrats seem to be choosing their words with care and accuracy. All they really need to do is quote the whistle-blowers complaint and the solicitor general's report in the full riveting power of each document. Planespoken words incriminating Trump almost as much as his own do. But what I really want to celebrate is a simple adverb that all in itself alone addresses the troubled and disturbed confusion of those who claim that in the teeth of the evidence, the transcript of the phone call, There was no Trump's statement that made clear there would be no defensive weapons for Ukraine unless Ukraine did his bidding. You know, quid pro quo. Ah, but there is. Other English majors who are at home analyzing the scansion of a Spencerian sonnet but unaccustomed to decoding documents affecting national security will understand that this is a bit of a thrill, especially since in the four days since the phone call transcript went public, no one seems to have pointed out the importance of this one word, at least not to my knowledge. And I'm a news junkie who reads and watches everything she can. But whether or not I'm the first to point this out. It needs pointing. It comes in the transcript just after the hapless Ukrainian president says, quote, I would also like to thank you for your great support in the area of defense. We are ready to continue to cooperate for the next steps. Specifically, we are almost ready to buy more javelins from the United States for defense purposes, close quote. Then Trump says, quote, I would like you to do us a favor, though, because our country has been through a lot, and Ukraine knows a lot about it, close quote. Yes, yes, earlier he's complained that his help for Ukraine had not been properly reciprocated, and later on he reiterates more of the same. But the key, the code, the smoking quid pro quo, resonate from the one word though. I would like you to do us a favor, though. Although and though both mean in spite of something, synonyms might be, however, nevertheless, nonetheless, despite and the like. Yes, but that would also work. These are subordinating conjunctions, meaning that the clause they introduce is a subordinate clause which needs a main clause to make it complete. In the case of though, though, the subordinate clause in effect negates the main clause. For example, main clause, she has a bad cold, subordinate clause, though she came to work this morning. Although and though make the previous main clause dependent on the subordinate clause, In fact, they overturn it. They force it to rely on the subordinate clause for its meaning. We need defensive weapons. I need a favor, though.
